old_entry.title: Carol Shaw and River Raid
old_entry.subtitle: A long flight inside four kilobytes
old_entry.summary: Carol Shaw needed more river than a cartridge could hold. She made the landscape from rules, then tuned those rules into a game.
body: The river keeps coming towards the player. Its banks narrow, obstacles interrupt the route, and the fuel gauge keeps falling. River Raid presents a long journey, but Carol Shaw had only a small cartridge in which to fit it. Storing a separate picture of every stretch of river was not an option.

For Activision's 1982 Atari 2600 game, Shaw used a repeatable number sequence to help decide the river's changing width. Short pieces of landscape could become a much longer course. Starting from the same value reproduced the same route, giving players a world they could learn rather than an arbitrary new river on every attempt.

The technical solution still needed a designer. Shaw adjusted how narrow the river could become and how often fuel appeared. Steering, shooting and refuelling pulled attention in different directions. A fuel depot could be an opportunity to survive longer, while a narrow channel punished an overcorrection. The landscape's apparent size mattered because it supported those decisions.

Her surviving papers preserve another side of the finished cartridge: code, working notes and design material. They let us follow the work behind the moving picture. A constraint became a method, and the method became something a player could feel as tension, rhythm and the possibility of making it a little farther upstream.

editorial_features.title: A river made from rules
editorial_features.summary: Shaw turned a repeatable terrain sequence into a controlled challenge.
body: River Raid had to provide a scrolling route within an Atari 2600 cartridge. Carol Shaw’s interview explains why the river could not simply be stored as a sequence of pictures. She used a repeatable sequence to generate terrain, then controlled what that process was allowed to produce. The method separates two things experienced together: the appearance of a continuous landscape and the rules creating it. Shaw was not merely reducing a picture until it fitted. She was deciding what information the machine actually needed to construct the flight.

Shaw’s papers at The Strong contain notes, sketches, design documents and source-code printouts. Its historical account describes Atari-era graphics drawn on graph paper and translated into numerical values, with code also written by hand before being entered. These materials preserve intermediate forms of work that a cartridge does not show. A small on-screen shape could begin as a marked square on paper; an instruction could exist first as handwriting. Following those forms makes the programmer’s decisions more visible than treating the finished display as something the computer produced alone.

Generating terrain did not settle the design. Shaw described restrictions on how narrow the river could become as the game progressed, turning an economical representation into a controlled challenge. Her conversation with Al Miller also helped move the idea away from another space setting. The aircraft, river and fuel created a different situation to read. This is where programming and design meet: the sequence supplies material, but the designer decides what kinds of passages it may produce and what the player must manage along the route.

The Strong identifies source printouts for River Raid among papers spanning Shaw’s work at Atari and Activision. The collection’s company-based arrangement places code alongside advertisements and career records. Access to some scans is managed by library staff because the connected paper requires care. A source listing is therefore instructions and an artifact that can be damaged or preserved. It gives a route toward understanding how the game was made, but its presence in an archive does not grant permission to reproduce the whole program.

old_entry.title: Fonz
old_entry.summary: Road Race is a 1976 racing video game developed and released by Sega in February 1976.
body: Road Race is a 1976 racing video game developed and released by Sega in February 1976. Later the same year, Sega released two motorbike racing variants, Man T.T. (released in August) and Moto-Cross, which were in turn re-branded as Fonz, in November 1976. The game was based on the character Fonzie (portrayed by Henry Winkler) from the 1970s TV show Happy Days, with the slogan being "TV's hottest name, Your hottest game". Sega licensed Fonz because at the time it was owned by Charles Bluhdorn's Gulf+Western Company and it was a Paramount Television intellectual property.
A two-player version of Man T.T. called Twin Course T.T. was released in January 1977.

Moto-Cross / Fonz is an early black-and-white motorbike racing game, most notable for introducing an early three-dimensional third-person perspective. Both versions of the game display a constantly changing forward-scrolling road and the player's bike in a third-person perspective where objects nearer to the player are larger than those nearer to the horizon, and the aim was to steer the vehicle across the road, racing against the clock, while avoiding any on-coming motorcycles or driving off the road. The game also introduced the use of haptic feedback, which caused the motorcycle handlebars to vibrate during a collision with another vehicle.

Fonz is a discrete logic system that uses more than 40 TTL intergrated circuits as opposed to a microprocessor. It also contains a ROM chip that contains the graphics of the motorcycle in various positions. An audio tape deck plays recorded sounds of motorcycle engines and crashes. To implement the way objects change size, the system changes its internal clock frequency, the rate at which the system operates, one each scanline of the display.
The general premise has the player controlling Fonzie on a motorcycle with handlebars on the cabinet.

The player has to go as fast as possible without skidding off the road or colliding with other racing bikes on the screen. Turn the handlebars, and the bike will corner and bank. Twist the handle throttle open, and it will accelerate. When a collision with another bike occurs, the handlebars vibrate and the screen flashes a reverse image. To increase the challenge, the size of the bike can be regulated by the operator.

In Japan, Road Race was among the top twenty highest-grossing arcade video games of 1976, according to the first annual Game Machine chart. In North America, Road Race was reported to be doing strong business upon release. Man T.T. was among the top ten highest-grossing arcade video games of 1977 in Japan.

Fonz was introduced at Chicago's Music Operators Association (MOA) show in November 1976. It was the first time that a television character was licensed for a video game, with Sega co-founder David M. Rosen predicting the start of a new coalition between the show business and amusement arcade industries. Sega also advertised the game for having both the road and bikes seen in "true perspective on the game screen, while the player operates realistically functioning handle-bars to simulate high-speed competition riding complete with authentic motor sounds". Sega said the response to the game at the MOA show was "unanimous and enthusiastic" and that test location results were very positive. At the start of December 1976, Sega of America reported that it had manufactured several hundred Fonz arcade cabinets.
